standard.title: Locate primary and secondary sources
standard.description: locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate, collect, and organise information from primary and secondary sources (AC9HS6S02). They have not yet applied the primary/secondary distinction specifically to historical inquiry — including the disciplinary definition of primary sources as sources from the time of the event being investigated, and the practical skills of locating sources in digital repositories and research databases.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry, demonstrating understanding of the primary/secondary distinction, ability to use search strategies to find sources in repositories and databases, and the capacity to sort and organise sources by type.

nodes.label: Primary and secondary sources — the disciplinary distinction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the distinction between primary and secondary sources as used in historical inquiry — primary sources are from the time of the event being investigated; secondary sources are later interpretations — and correctly classify a given set of sources.
nodes.minimum_width: Define primary and secondary sources using the disciplinary definition, and correctly classify at least four given sources (a mix of obvious and less obvious examples).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the distinction between primary and secondary sources — primary sources are from the time of the event (scrolls, coins, artefacts, artwork, inscriptions, human remains); secondary sources are later interpretations of the past — and correctly classify a range of source types including edge cases (e.g. a modern translation of an ancient text, a photograph of an artefact).
wider: Examine edge cases that challenge the primary/secondary distinction — a modern translation of an ancient text (primary content, secondary medium?), a later copy of a lost original, a documentary that uses primary source footage — and discuss how historians navigate these ambiguities.

Investigate how the primary/secondary distinction differs across disciplines — in science, a 'primary source' means something different than in history — and why the historical definition is tied to the concept of 'from the time of the event'.

Explore how the same object can function as both a primary source (evidence about the time it was made) and a secondary source (evidence about how later people interpreted the past) depending on the inquiry question.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who misclassify sources based on age rather than temporal relationship to the event being studied will produce systematically wrong source organisation in N3 and import the error into S03–S04 source analysis work — all downstream source skills depend on reliable primary/secondary classification.

response_modes.reason: The primary/secondary distinction is a precision skill with common errors — students frequently classify based on medium (old = primary, modern = secondary) rather than temporal relationship to the event being studied. Regular practice classifying a variety of sources, including deliberate edge cases, builds the precision needed before source analysis work in S03–S04 can proceed reliably.

success_criteria: States the correct disciplinary definition of primary and secondary sources (primary = from the time of the event).
Correctly classifies at least four sources, including at least one non-obvious case.
Does not classify based on age alone — recognises that a modern document about a modern event is still a primary source.

nodes.label: Locating sources — repositories and search strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate primary and secondary sources using digital repositories, archives, and research databases, applying appropriate search strategies to find relevant evidence for a historical inquiry question.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a digital repository or search tool to locate at least one primary and one secondary source relevant to a historical inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Locate primary and secondary sources using digital repositories (e.g. museum collections, archival databases, library catalogues) and research databases, applying search strategies such as filtering by source type, using subject-specific keywords, and selecting search terms relevant to the inquiry question.
wider: Investigate how different repositories specialise in different source types — museum collections for artefacts, national archives for government documents, digital humanities projects for ancient texts — and develop strategies for knowing where to look for different types of evidence.

Examine how digital repositories of archaeological sources and records can be searched using subject filters; for example, searching Rome ceramics + religion to find relevant artefacts, and what the search results reveal about the type and scope of available evidence.

Explore the difference between a Google search and a disciplinary repository search — examining why historians use specialised databases and what is lost when research is limited to general web searches.

response_modes.reason: Locating sources across different repository types — museum collections, archival databases, library catalogues — requires practice with different interfaces, search filters, and keyword strategies. Students need repeated exposure to different repository types before they can independently identify which tool is appropriate for a given source type and apply effective search strategies.

success_criteria: Successfully locates at least one primary and one secondary source relevant to a given inquiry question.
Identifies the repository or database used and explains why it was appropriate for the source type sought.
Uses subject-specific search terms rather than general keyword searches.

nodes.label: Sorting and organising sources for inquiry
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can sort and organise a set of primary and secondary sources by type, identify categories relevant to their inquiry, and explain why different source types serve different purposes in a historical investigation.
nodes.minimum_width: Sort a given set of sources into primary and secondary categories and identify two or three category types within the primary sources (e.g. artefacts, written records, visual sources).
nodes.typical_width: Sort and organise a set of sources by type — distinguishing primary sources by medium (artefacts, written records, visual sources, oral/aural sources) and secondary sources by purpose (historical analysis, popular history, reference) — and explain how each category of source serves a different function in historical inquiry.
wider: Develop a source management system for a sustained historical inquiry — creating a way of organising, noting, and retrieving sources that supports the inquiry process rather than just accumulating materials.

Examine how different categories of primary sources (archaeological vs written vs oral) have different strengths and limitations for different inquiry questions — developing criteria for selecting which source types are most appropriate for a given question.

Investigate how the availability of different source types varies by historical period and place — examining why some ancient societies are better documented than others and what this means for the questions historians can ask.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the primary/secondary distinction (Node 1) and locating skills (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand — identifying and organising sources to use in inquiry. Students must coordinate the disciplinary categories with practical organisation and explain how source types serve different inquiry functions, connecting the skill to the purposes of historical investigation.

success_criteria: Correctly sorts a set of sources into primary and secondary categories.
Identifies at least two sub-categories within primary sources (e.g. artefact, written, visual).
Explains why different source types serve different functions in historical inquiry.
